explanation.en:
The position of the verb shows the clause type.
In a main clause the conjugated verb is in second position; in a subordinate clause (after dass, weil, wenn, ob etc.) it goes to the end.
Example: Er bleibt zu Hause, weil er krank ist.
He stays at home because he is ill.

rule.en:
1. Main clause: verb in position 2
In a German main clause, the conjugated verb always stands in position 2 — no matter what occupies position 1 (subject, time expression, object, etc.). This is called verb-second order.

Ich lese heute ein Buch.
I'm reading a book today.
(position 1: subject)
Heute lese ich ein Buch. (position 1: time expression — the subject shifts to position 3!)
Ein Buch lese ich heute. (position 1: object)

Important: only one sentence element ever stands before the verb — no matter how long it is.

2. Subordinate clause: verb at the end
After subordinating conjunctions such as dass, weil, wenn, ob, obwohl, während, nachdem, bevor, da, damit, sodass, als, the conjugated verb moves all the way to the end of the clause.

Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin.
I'm staying home because I'm sick.
Sie fragt, ob er morgen kommt.
She asks whether he's coming tomorrow.

3. Sentence bracket with two verb parts
When there are two verb parts (perfect tense, modal verb + infinitive, separable verb), they form a sentence bracket (Satzklammer): the conjugated part stands at the front, the second part at the very end.

Main clause: Ich habe das Buch gelesen.
I have read the book.
Main clause: Ich muss das Buch lesen.
I must read the book.
Main clause: Ich rufe dich morgen an.
I'll call you tomorrow.

Subordinate clause: ..., weil ich das Buch gelesen habe.
Subordinate clause: ..., weil ich das Buch lesen muss.
Subordinate clause: ..., weil ich dich morgen anrufe.

4. Questions
Yes / no question — verb in position 1: Kommst du morgen?
Are you coming tomorrow?
Wh-question — question word in position 1, verb in position 2: Wann kommst du?
When are you coming?

5. Conjunctions in „position 0“
The conjunctions und, oder, aber, denn, sondern join two main clauses but do not count as a sentence element, so the verb stays in second position. Compare „denn“ (main clause) with „weil“ (subordinate clause):

Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn ich bin krank.
I'm staying at home, because I'm ill.

Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin.
I'm staying at home because I'm ill.

explanation.en:
Kein or nicht? It depends on what is being negated.
„Kein“ negates a noun with an indefinite article or no article: Ich habe keine Zeit.
I have no time.
„Nicht“ negates everything else — verbs, adjectives, nouns with a definite article, whole sentences: Er kommt heute nicht.
He is not coming today.

rule.en:
1. Kein — negating the noun
Kein replaces the indefinite article „ein / eine“ or negates a noun that has no article at all (plurals, uncountable nouns). It's declined exactly like „ein“.

Ich habe einen Bruder. → Ich habe keinen Bruder.
I have no brother.

Ich trinke Kaffee. → Ich trinke keinen Kaffee.
I don't drink coffee.

Das sind Probleme. → Das sind keine Probleme.
These are not problems.

2. Nicht — negating everything else
„Nicht“ negates verbs, adjectives, adverbs, nouns with a definite article / possessive, and whole sentences. Its position depends on what is being negated.

CasePosition of „nicht“
Sentence negationas far back as possible: at the end of the sentence — or directly before the second verb part, an adjective or a prepositional phrase
Er kommt heute nicht.
He is not coming today.
Ich habe das Buch nicht gelesen.
I haven't read the book.
Er ruft mich nicht an.
He doesn't call me.
Sie ist nicht müde.
She isn't tired.
Ich interessiere mich nicht für Politik.
I'm not interested in politics.
Partial negationdirectly before the negated word — often with „sondern“
Er kommt nicht heute, sondern morgen.
He's not coming today, but tomorrow.

3. Careful with nouns: kein or nicht?
Nouns with an indefinite article or no article → „kein“. Nouns with a definite article, a possessive or a name → „nicht“. Abstract nouns without an article and professions are also negated with „kein“.

Ich habe kein Auto.
I don't have a car.

Ich kenne den Mann nicht.
I don't know the man.

Das ist nicht mein Auto.
That isn't my car.

Er ist kein Arzt.
He isn't a doctor.

Ich habe keine Ahnung.
I have no idea.

Ich habe keine Lust.
I don't feel like it.

4. No double negation
Words such as nie, niemals, niemand, nichts, nirgends already contain the negation. Unlike in Ukrainian, Russian and many other languages, no additional „nicht“ is added. With nouns, „noch nicht“ and „nicht mehr“ become „noch kein“ and „kein … mehr“.

Ich habe niemanden gesehen. (nicht: „Ich habe niemanden nicht gesehen.“)
I didn't see anyone.

Ich habe noch nicht gegessen.
I haven't eaten yet.

Ich habe noch kein Auto.
I don't have a car yet.

Ich habe kein Geld mehr.
I have no money left.

explanation.en:
Two parts, one connector — they always belong together.
„entweder … oder“ (one of two options), „sowohl … als auch“ (both), „weder … noch“ (neither), „nicht nur … sondern auch“ (more than expected), „zwar … aber“ (concession and limitation).
Example: Er hat weder Zeit noch Lust.
He has neither time nor desire.

rule.en:
Overview of the most important two-part connectors

ConnectorMeaning
entweder ... oderone of two options
Entweder fliegen wir, oder wir fahren mit dem Zug.
Either we fly, or we take the train.
sowohl ... als auchboth together, no contrast
Sie spricht sowohl Deutsch als auch Französisch.
She speaks both German and French.
weder ... nochneither of the two (negates both)
Er hat weder Zeit noch Lust.
He has neither time nor desire.
nicht nur ... sondern auchmore than expected, an increase
Er ist nicht nur pünktlich, sondern auch zuverlässig.
He is not only punctual but also reliable.
zwar ... aberconcession + limitation
Zwar ist das Projekt teuer, aber es lohnt sich.
Although the project is expensive, it's worth it.

1. Sentence structure: position 1 and position 0
If the first part comes first („entweder“, „zwar“), it counts as position 1 — the verb follows directly. The second part („oder“, „aber“) is in position 0: the normal word order continues after it.

Entweder kommt er heute, oder er kommt gar nicht.
Either he comes today, or he does not come at all.

Zwar regnet es, aber wir gehen trotzdem raus.
Although it's raining, we're going out anyway.

2. „Weder … noch“ already contains the negation
No additional „nicht“ or „kein“ is added:

Er kann weder kochen noch backen. (nicht: „Er kann nicht weder kochen noch backen.“)
He can neither cook nor bake.

3. The verb with „sowohl … als auch“
When two subjects are joined, the verb is in the plural:

Sowohl mein Kollege als auch ich waren dabei.
Both my colleague and I were there.

4. Comma rule
A comma always stands before „sondern“ and „aber“, because a contrast follows. Before „oder“ and „noch“ there is a comma only when two complete clauses are joined — not with single words or phrases.

Zwar regnet es, aber wir gehen trotzdem raus.
Although it's raining, we're going out anyway.

Entweder fliegen wir, oder wir fahren mit dem Zug. (zwei Sätze → Komma)
Either we fly, or we take the train.

Er hat weder Zeit noch Lust. (Wörter → kein Komma)
He has neither time nor desire.

title.en: um zu / ohne zu / (an)statt zu + infinitive

explanation.en:
Same subject → infinitive clause with „zu“.
„um … zu“ states a goal, „ohne … zu“ something that is missing or does not happen, „(an)statt … zu“ an alternative. With different subjects use „damit“, „ohne dass“, „anstatt dass“.
Example: Ich lerne, um die Prüfung zu bestehen.
I study in order to pass the exam.

rule.en:
1. Basic condition: the same subject
Infinitive constructions with „zu“ only work when the main clause and the subordinate part share the same subject. If not, you need the corresponding subordinate-clause variant with „dass“.

ConstructionQuestion / other variant
um ... zuWhat for? With what goal?
other variant: damit
ohne ... zuWithout doing what?
other variant: ohne dass
(an)statt ... zuInstead of doing what?
other variant: anstatt dass

2. Examples with the same subject (infinitive with zu)
Ich lerne, um die Prüfung zu bestehen. (I study = I pass the exam)
Er ging, ohne sich zu verabschieden. (he left = he doesn't say goodbye)
Sie arbeitet, anstatt zu schlafen. (she works = she doesn't sleep)

3. Examples with different subjects (dass-clause)
Ich gebe dir das Buch, damit du es liest. (I give / you read — two different subjects)
Er ging, ohne dass jemand es bemerkte.
He left without anyone noticing.

Sie arbeitet weiter, anstatt dass die anderen ihr helfen.
She keeps working instead of the others helping her.

4. Position of „zu“ with separable verbs
With separable verbs, „zu“ goes between the prefix and the stem:
um die Prüfung abzuschließen
in order to complete the exam

5. Comma and „damit“
A comma always stands before an infinitive clause with „um … zu“, „ohne … zu“ and „(an)statt … zu“. With the same subject „um … zu“ is the normal choice; „damit“ is also possible but sounds heavier:

Ich lerne, damit ich die Prüfung bestehe.
I study so that I pass the exam.

title.en: Comparative clauses: als, wie, je…desto / umso

explanation.en:
Three words, three types of comparison.
„Wie“ compares equals (so tall wie), „als“ compares unequals after the comparative (taller als), „je … desto / umso“ + comparative shows: when one thing rises, the other rises (or falls) too.
Example: Je mehr er übt, desto besser wird er.
The more he practises, the better he gets.

rule.en:
Overview
WordType / adjective form after it
wieequality (so ... wie)
after it: positive form
alsinequality
after it: comparative form
je ... desto / umsoproportionality
after it: two comparatives

1. Wie — equality
Pattern: so + adjective (positive form) + wie.
Er ist so groß wie sein Vater.
He is as tall as his father.

Negated:
Er ist nicht so groß wie sein Vater.
He isn't as tall as his father.

2. Als — inequality
After a comparative, it's always „als“, never „wie“:
Er ist größer als sein Vater.
He is taller than his father. (not: „größer wie“ — a common colloquial mistake!)

3. Je … desto / umso — proportion
Two clauses are linked: the first (with „je“) is a subordinate clause — verb at the end. The second (with „desto“ / „umso“) is a main clause: „desto / umso + comparative“ is in position 1 and the verb follows directly. „Desto“ and „umso“ mean the same.

Je mehr er übt, desto besser wird er.
The more he practises, the better he gets.

Je früher wir anfangen, umso schneller sind wir fertig.
The earlier we start, the sooner we are done.

4. More patterns with „wie“ and „als“
genauso / ebenso … wie stresses complete equality. anders / etwas anderes / nichts anderes take „als“. When comparing with a whole clause, a comma is used and the verb goes to the end:

Er ist genauso groß wie sein Vater.
He is just as tall as his father.

Das ist etwas anderes als vorher.
That is something different from before.

Das Projekt ist teurer, als wir dachten.
The project is more expensive than we thought.

Die Prüfung war nicht so schwer, wie ich befürchtet hatte.
The exam wasn't as hard as I had feared.

explanation.en:
„Es“ has three jobs — often without a meaning of its own.
1) impersonal with weather, time and fixed expressions: Es regnet. (It is raining.)
2) placeholder in position 1: Es freut mich, dass du kommst. (I am glad that you are coming.)
3) correlate pointing to a following subordinate clause: Ich finde es toll, dass du kommst. (I think it is great that you are coming.)

rule.en:
1. Es as an impersonal pronoun
With weather, time of day, and some fixed expressions there's no „real“ subject — „es“ fills that slot:
Es regnet.
It's raining.
Es ist spät.
It's late.
Es gibt viele Möglichkeiten.
There are many options.
Es geht mir gut.
I'm doing well.
This „es“ never disappears, not even when word order changes: Heute regnet es.
Today it's raining.

2. Es as a placeholder (Vorfeld-es)
When the actual subject (often a dass-clause or infinitive) doesn't yet stand at the start of the sentence, „es“ stands as a placeholder in position 1 — it disappears as soon as something else takes position 1.

Es freut mich, dass du kommst. → Dass du kommst, freut mich. (no more „es“!)
It makes me happy that you're coming. → That you're coming makes me happy.
Es ist wichtig, pünktlich zu sein. → Pünktlich zu sein ist wichtig.
It is important to be punctual. → Being punctual is important.

3. Es as a correlate (pointing to a subordinate clause)
The correlate „es“ points to a dass-clause or infinitive clause that follows. If the subordinate clause comes first, „es“ is dropped.

Ich finde es toll, dass du kommst.
I think it's great that you're coming.

Dass du kommst, finde ich toll. (kein „es“ mehr!)
That you're coming, I think is great.

Er hasst es, früh aufzustehen.
He hates getting up early.

4. Fixed expressions with „es“
In expressions such as es gibt, es geht um, es handelt sich um, es kommt auf … an, „es“ is a fixed part of the phrase — it stays even when the word order changes:

In diesem Text geht es um Geld.
This text is about money.

Hier gibt es viele Möglichkeiten.
There are many possibilities here.

5. Test: what happens when the word order changes?
ObservationFunction
„es“ always staysimpersonal or fixed „es“
Heute regnet es.
It's raining today.
„es“ disappears when the subject moves to position 1placeholder
Es kamen viele Gäste. → Viele Gäste kamen.
Many guests came.
Es wurde viel gelacht. → Gestern wurde viel gelacht.
There was a lot of laughter yesterday.
„es“ disappears when the subordinate clause moves to the frontcorrelate
Ich finde es toll, dass du kommst. → Dass du kommst, finde ich toll.
I think it's great that you're coming.

explanation.en:
Here „wer“ means „whoever …“ — with no antecedent.
The „wer“-clause is a subordinate clause (verb at the end). The main clause often continues with a correlate („der“ / „den“ / „dem“) whose case depends on its role in the main clause.
Example: Wer zu spät kommt, der verpasst den Zug.
Whoever comes too late misses the train.

rule.en:
1. Structure: wer-clause + correlate clause
A „wer“-clause is a subordinate clause (verb at the end) that needs no reference noun and means „the one who...“. It is followed by a main clause that often begins with an article word (der / den / dem) referring back to „wer“ — the correlate.

Wer zu spät kommt, verpasst den Zug.
Whoever comes late misses the train.
Wer fragt, der lernt.
Whoever asks, learns.

2. The correlate follows the case in the main clause
The correlate takes whatever case it needs in the main clause.

CaseCorrelate
Nominativeder
Wer fragt, der lernt.
Whoever asks, learns.
Accusativeden
Wer zu spät kommt, den lässt man nicht mehr rein.
Whoever comes late is no longer let in.
Dativedem
Wer clever ist, dem gelingt es leicht.
Whoever is clever finds it easy to succeed.

3. „wer“ has case forms of its own
„wer“ changes too: wer (nominative), wen (accusative), wem (dative) — depending on its role in the subordinate clause. So the case of „wer“ and the case of the correlate are independent of each other.

Wem das nicht passt, der kann gehen.
Whoever doesn't like it can leave.
(„wem“ = dative in the subordinate clause, „der“ = nominative in the main clause)

4. When can the correlate be dropped?
The correlate can be dropped when „wer“ and the correlate are in the same case. If they are in different cases, the correlate must stay.

Wer zu spät kommt, verpasst den Zug. (statt: …, der verpasst den Zug.)
Whoever comes too late misses the train.

Wer zu spät kommt, den lässt man nicht mehr rein. (Nominativ ≠ Akkusativ → Korrelat bleibt)
Whoever comes too late is no longer let in.

5. Similar: „was“
„Was“ can be used in the same way — for things and generalisations:

Was er sagt, das stimmt.
What he says is true.

explanation.en:
A fixed combination of a noun and an „empty“ verb — the meaning lies in the noun.
You learn them as a whole, including the preposition and article. They are typical of formal, professional texts; in everyday speech people often use the simple verb.
Example: Das Gesetz tritt am 1. Januar in Kraft. (= gilt ab dem 1. Januar)
The law comes into force on 1 January.

rule.en:
1. What is a noun-verb collocation (NVV)?
A fixed combination of a noun (usually with a preposition) + a semantically „empty“ verb (treten, finden, stehen, kommen, bringen, geben, nehmen ...). The meaning often corresponds to a single full verb.

NVVMeaning
in Kraft tretengelten
to take effect
Das Gesetz tritt am 1. Januar in Kraft.
The law takes effect on 1 January.
Anwendung findenangewendet werden
to be applied
Die neue Methode findet breite Anwendung.
The new method is widely applied.
zur Verfügung stehenverfügbar sein
to be available
Der Berater steht Ihnen zur Verfügung.
The consultant is at your disposal.
eine Entscheidung treffenentscheiden
to decide
Der Vorstand trifft die Entscheidung.
The board makes the decision.
in Betracht ziehenerwägen
to consider
Wir ziehen diese Option in Betracht.
We are considering this option.

2. Why does it matter?
Noun-verb collocations are typical of formal, professional and written texts (reports, contracts, news). They sound more formal than the simple full verb — in everyday speech people usually say gelten rather than in Kraft sein. At work you need to understand them and use them appropriately.

3. The preposition and article are fixed
In these collocations the preposition and article (or the lack of one) are fixed — nothing can be replaced:

zur Verfügung stehen (nicht: „an der Verfügung“)
to be available

in Kraft treten (nicht: „auf Kraft“)
to come into force

4. The verb shows the perspective
The verb in the collocation changes how the noun is meant:

VerbsMeaning
treten / kommen / geratensomething begins or arises
in Kraft treten
to come into force
in Schwierigkeiten geraten
to get into difficulties
setzen / bringen / stellensomeone causes something
ein Gesetz in Kraft setzen
to put a law into force
zum Abschluss bringen
to bring to a conclusion
zur Diskussion stellen
to put up for discussion
stehen / sein / bleibena state exists
zur Verfügung stehen
to be available
in Betrieb sein
to be in operation


Many collocations with „kommen“ or „finden“ have a passive meaning:

Die neue Methode kommt zur Anwendung. (= wird angewendet)
The new method is being applied.

explanation.en:
The passive puts the action, not the actor, in the centre.
Process passive: werden + past participle. Passive substitutes (similar meaning, often expressing possibility): „sich lassen + infinitive“, „sein + zu + infinitive“ or a „man“ construction.
Example: Das Auto wird repariert. / Das lässt sich reparieren.
The car is being repaired. / That can be repaired.

rule.en:
1. The true dynamic passive
Formation: werden (conjugated) + past participle (at the end of the clause). It describes a process, not the result.

TenseExample
PresentDas Auto wird repariert.
The car is being repaired.
Simple pastDas Auto wurde repariert.
The car was repaired.
Present perfectDas Auto ist repariert worden.
The car has been repaired.
With modal verbDas Auto muss repariert werden.
The car must be repaired.

2. Naming the agent: von / durch
If you do want to name the person performing the action, use „von“ (person / originator) or „durch“ (means / cause):
Das Auto wird von einem Mechaniker repariert.
The car is repaired by a mechanic.
Der Schaden wurde durch den Sturm verursacht.
The damage was caused by the storm.

3. Passive substitutes — three alternatives with modal meaning
FormMeaning
sich lassen + infinitivepossibility (can be)
Das Problem lässt sich lösen.
The problem can be solved.
sein + zu + infinitivepossibility OR necessity
Das Problem ist zu lösen.
The problem is to be / can be solved.
man + active clauseneutral, everyday style
Man löst das Problem.
One solves the problem.

4. Why use the passive / passive substitute?
Typical of reports, instructions, and scientific texts, when the focus is on the action or the object rather than on the person carrying it out.

5. Two more options
sein + adjective ending in -bar / -lich expresses possibility. bekommen / erhalten + past participle (the bekommen passive) turns the dative object into the subject:

Das Problem ist lösbar. (= Das Problem kann gelöst werden.)
The problem is solvable.

Sie bekommt die Rechnung geschickt. (= Die Rechnung wird ihr geschickt.)
She is sent the invoice.

explanation.en:
Indefinite pronouns refer to people or quantities without specifying them exactly.
For people: man, jemand, niemand. For things and quantities: etwas, nichts, alle, jeder, einige, manche. Most of them are declined.
Example: Ich habe niemanden gesehen. (Akkusativ)
I didn't see anyone. (accusative)

rule.en:
1. For people
PronounMeaning
mansomeone, in general
Nom. / Acc. / Dat.: man / einen / einem
jemandan unspecified person
Nom. / Acc. / Dat.: jemand / jemanden / jemandem
niemandno person
Nom. / Acc. / Dat.: niemand / niemanden / niemandem

„Man“ is never declined like a normal pronoun — in the accusative / dative it becomes „einen“ / „einem“:
Das ärgert einen wirklich.
That really annoys you / one.
In everyday speech, „jemand“ / „niemand“ can also drop the -en / -em endings:
Ich habe niemand(en) gesehen.
I saw no one.

2. For things and quantities
PronounMeaning
etwas / nichtssomething / nothing (invariable)
Declension: no endings
alleall (plural)
Declension: like the definite article
jedereach one (singular)
Declension: like „dieser“
einige / manchean indefinite quantity
Declension: like the definite article (plural)

3. Examples by case
Ich habe niemanden gesehen.
I saw no one. (accusative)

Ich habe allen geholfen.
I helped everyone. (dative)

Das interessiert jeden.
That interests everyone. (accusative)

4. Adjective after „etwas“ / „nichts“
After „etwas“, „nichts“, „viel“ and „wenig“ the adjective is capitalised and has strong endings (as without an article): nominative / accusative -es, dative -em.

Das ist etwas Interessantes.
That is something interesting.

Ich habe nichts Neues gehört.
I haven't heard anything new.

Er arbeitet an etwas Neuem.
He is working on something new.

5. With „irgend-“ it becomes even less specific
With „irgend-“ you show that it does not matter who or what: irgendjemand, irgendetwas, irgendein.

Hat irgendjemand meinen Schlüssel gesehen?
Has anyone seen my key?

title.en: als ob / als wenn + Konjunktiv II

explanation.en:
Unreal comparison: you act as if something were true — but it is not.
„als ob“ / „als wenn“ + subordinate clause (verb at the end) in Konjunktiv II. With „als“ alone the verb follows directly.
Example: Er tut, als ob er alles wüsste. / Er tut, als wüsste er alles.
He acts as if he knew everything.

rule.en:
1. Two variants: with and without „ob“ / „wenn“
ConstructionWord order
als ob / als wennsubordinate clause: verb at the end
Er tut, als ob er alles wüsste.
He acts as if he knew everything.
als (alone)verb right after „als“
Er tut, als wüsste er alles.
He acts as if he knew everything.

Both variants mean the same thing — the short form with „als“ + verb (word order as in a main clause) is somewhat more elegant / literary.

2. Why Konjunktiv II?
The comparison doesn't match reality — you're expressing: „He acts this way, but in reality it's different.“ This is the typical use of Konjunktiv II for unreal situations.

3. Present vs. past
Time referenceForm
PresentKonjunktiv II Präsens
Sie tut, als ob sie krank wäre.
She acts as if she were sick.
PastKonjunktiv II Perfekt
Sie tut, als ob sie krank gewesen wäre.
She acts as if she had been sick.

Präsens: the simple form or „würde“ + infinitive.
Perfekt: „hätte“ / „wäre“ + past participle.

4. Common verbs in this construction
sein → wäre,
haben → hätte,
können → könnte,
wissen → wüsste,
kommen → käme.
For most other verbs, spoken German uses „würde“ + infinitive:
als ob er schlafen würde.
as if he were sleeping.

5. Typical lead-ins
The „als ob“ clause often follows „so tun“, „aussehen“, „klingen“, „wirken“ or „scheinen“:

Es sieht aus, als ob es bald regnen würde.
It looks as if it were going to rain soon.

Das klingt, als wäre er unzufrieden.
That sounds as if he were dissatisfied.

explanation.en:
The stative passive describes the result, not the process.
Formation: sein + past participle. Who acted does not matter.
Example: Die Tür wird geöffnet. (Vorgang) / Die Tür ist geöffnet. (Zustand)
The door is being opened. (process) / The door is open. (state)

rule.en:
1. Two types of passive compared
TypeFormation
Dynamic passive (Vorgangspassiv)werden + past participle
Meaning: process, action underway
Die Tür wird geöffnet.
The door is being opened.
Statal passive (Zustandspassiv)sein + past participle
Meaning: state, result of the action
Die Tür ist geöffnet.
The door is open.

2. The test: „happening right now“ vs. „already done“
Can you insert „right now“? → dynamic passive. Are you only describing the state afterward, with no one actively performing the action? → statal passive.

Das Geschäft wird um 8 Uhr geöffnet. (Process: someone opens it at 8 o'clock.)
Das Geschäft ist ab 8 Uhr geöffnet. (State: it's open from 8 o'clock on, regardless of who opened it.)

3. Tenses of the statal passive
TenseExample
PresentDer Laden ist geschlossen.
The shop is closed.
Simple pastDer Laden war geschlossen.
The shop was closed.
Present perfectDer Laden ist geschlossen gewesen.
The shop has been closed.

4. No agent (no „von“ phrase)
In the statal passive, you almost never name who performed the action — the focus is exclusively on the subject's current state.

5. Careful: „ist geöffnet“ ≠ „ist geöffnet worden“
The perfect of the process passive is formed with „sein“ + past participle + „worden“. It describes a completed process, not a state:

Die Tür ist geöffnet worden. (Vorgang, vorbei: Jemand hat sie geöffnet.)
The door was opened.

Die Tür ist geöffnet. (Zustand: Sie ist jetzt offen.)
The door is open.

explanation.en:
A text holds together when its sentences are linked by references.
This is done with connectors (deshalb, außerdem), pronouns, synonyms and da- compounds: dabei (meanwhile), dadurch (because of this fact), dazu (in addition), davon (out of this group), damit (with this measure).
Example: Die Firma wächst. Dabei hilft die neue Strategie.
The company is growing. The new strategy helps with this.

rule.en:
1. Devices for linking a text together
DeviceFunction
Connectorslogical link between sentences
deshalb, außerdem, jedoch
Pronounsreplace a noun already mentioned
er, sie, es, dieser
Synonymsavoid repeating a word
die Firma → das Unternehmen
da-compoundsrefer back to a whole situation
dabei, dadurch, dazu, davon, damit

2. The da(r)- compounds in detail
These words replace „preposition + thing“ and refer to a noun or to a whole situation:

WordMeaning
dabeimeanwhile / in this context
Die Firma wächst. Dabei hilft die neue Strategie.
The company is growing. The new strategy helps with this.
dadurchbecause of this fact / by this means
Er hat viel gearbeitet. Dadurch hatte er Erfolg.
He worked a lot. As a result he was successful.
dazuin addition / on this subject
Wir haben zu wenig Zeit. Dazu fehlt uns das Budget.
We have too little time. On top of that we lack the budget.
davonof this / out of this group
Wir haben drei Angebote. Davon ist eines sehr günstig.
We have three offers. One of them is very cheap.
damitwith this / by this measure
Wir ändern den Ablauf. Damit sparen wir Zeit.
We're changing the process. This saves us time.

3. Things and people
The da(r)- compounds are used only for things and situations. For people, the preposition is used with a noun or pronoun. Before a vowel „dar-“ is used instead of „da-“: darauf, darüber, darin.

Wir planen ein Projekt. Ich freue mich darauf. (Sache)
We're planning a project. I'm looking forward to it.

Ich freue mich auf meinen Kollegen. (Person)
I'm looking forward to seeing my colleague.

4. Why does it matter for B2 / C1 texts?
These reference words make a text more compact and avoid constantly repeating whole parts of sentences — typical of good reports and essays.

explanation.en:
„Indem“ and „dadurch, dass“ answer the question: In what way?
They name the means. „Indem“ is shorter and more common (usually the same subject in both clauses); „dadurch, dass“ is more formal and stresses the means. The verb goes to the end.
Example: Er lernte die Sprache, indem er viel las.
He learned the language by reading a lot.

rule.en:
1. Two forms for „in what way?“
ConnectorStyle
indemshorter, more common
Er lernte die Sprache, indem er viel las.
He learned the language by reading a lot.
dadurch, dassmore formal, stresses the means
Er lernte die Sprache dadurch, dass er viel las.
He learned the language by reading a lot.

Both are subordinate clauses — the conjugated verb stands at the end: ..., indem er viel las.

2. Distinguishing from „weil“
„Weil“ states a reason / cause (why?), while „indem“ / „dadurch, dass“ state a means / method (by what means, in what way?). Compare:
Er ist müde, weil er viel gearbeitet hat.
He's tired because he worked a lot. (reason)
Er wurde erfolgreich, indem er viel gearbeitet hat.
He became successful by working a lot. (method)

3. The subject in the main and subordinate clause
„Indem“ is mostly used when both clauses have the same subject. If the subjects differ, use „dadurch, dass“:

Er lernte die Sprache, indem er viel las. (er … er)
He learned the language by reading a lot.

Die Firma spart Kosten, dadurch, dass die Mitarbeiter von zu Hause arbeiten. (Firma … Mitarbeiter)
The company saves costs by having its employees work from home.

4. Alternative: „durch“ + noun
„Durch“ + a nominalisation is a preposition (not a subordinate clause). If you need a whole clause with a verb, use „indem“ or „dadurch, dass“:

Durch viel Lesen lernte er die Sprache.
He learned the language through a lot of reading.

5. Position in the sentence
The modal clause can come before or after the main clause. If it comes first, the main-clause verb follows directly (position 2):

Indem er viel las, lernte er die Sprache.
By reading a lot, he learned the language.

title.en: Fixed prepositions with nouns / verbs / adjectives

explanation.en:
Many verbs, nouns and adjectives require a fixed preposition with a fixed case.
Both must be learned as a whole — the preposition cannot be derived from the meaning.
Example: sich interessieren für + Akk. (nicht: „an“), stolz sein auf + Akk., Angst vor + Dat.
to be interested in (not „an“), to be proud of, fear of

rule.en:
1. Verbs with a fixed preposition (examples)
VerbPreposition + case
sich interessierenfür + acc.
Ich interessiere mich für Kunst.
I'm interested in art.
wartenauf + acc.
Ich warte auf den Bus.
I'm waiting for the bus.
sich freuenüber + acc. / auf + acc.
Ich freue mich über das Geschenk. / auf die Reise.
I'm happy about the gift. / I'm looking forward to the trip.
denkenan + acc.
Ich denke an dich.
I'm thinking of you.

2. Adjectives with a fixed preposition
AdjectivePreposition + case
stolzauf + acc.
Sie ist stolz auf ihre Arbeit.
She's proud of her work.
zufriedenmit + dat.
Er ist zufrieden mit dem Ergebnis.
He's satisfied with the result.

3. Nouns with a fixed preposition
NounPreposition + case
die Angstvor + dat.
Angst vor der Prüfung
fear of the exam
das Interessean + dat.
Interesse an Sprachen
interest in languages

4. Important
„An“, „auf“, „über“ don't change their case depending on meaning here — with governed prepositions (Rektion), the case is fixed, regardless of the usual two-way preposition rule (Where? = dative, Where to? = accusative).

5. Learning tip
Always learn these as a whole unit: not just „warten“, but „warten auf + acc.“ — ideally together with an example sentence.

6. Asking and referring: „worauf“ / „darauf“
For things, you ask with „wo(r)- + preposition“ and refer back with „da(r)- + preposition“. For people, the preposition stays with the question word or pronoun. A dass-clause or infinitive clause can follow:

Worauf wartest du? — Ich warte darauf. (Sache)
What are you waiting for? — I am waiting for it.

Auf wen wartest du? — Ich warte auf meinen Freund. (Person)
Who are you waiting for? — I am waiting for my friend.

Ich warte darauf, dass der Bus kommt.
I'm waiting for the bus to come.

explanation.en:
Konjunktiv I signals: I did not say this, I am only reporting it.
Typical of news and reports. If the Konjunktiv I form is identical to the indicative, Konjunktiv II is used instead.
Example: Er sagte, er sei krank.
He said that he was ill.

rule.en:
1. Formation of Konjunktiv I
Present-tense stem + endings: -e, -est, -e, -en, -et, -en. Only „sein“ is irregular: ich sei, du seist, er / sie / es sei, wir seien, ihr seiet, sie seien.

Verber / sie / es
sagener sage
habener habe
könnener könne

2. When does Konjunktiv I → Konjunktiv II?
With „ich“, „wir“, and „sie“ (plural), Konjunktiv I often looks exactly like the indicative (e.g., „ich sage“, „sie sagen“) — so in those cases speakers switch to Konjunktiv II to keep reported speech recognizable:
Sie sagten, sie würden kommen.
They said they would come. (instead of „sie kommen“, which wouldn't be recognizable as a subjunctive)

3. Time relationships
Time referenceForm
SimultaneousKonjunktiv I Präsens
Er sagt, er sei müde.
He says he is tired.
PriorKonjunktiv I Perfekt
Er sagt, er sei müde gewesen.
He says he was tired.

Perfekt: „habe“ / „sei“ + past participle.

4. Verbs that introduce reported speech
Typical after: sagen, behaupten, berichten, erklären, betonen, meinen — often with „dass“ or without it (in which case main-clause word order applies):
Er sagte, dass er krank sei. / Er sagte, er sei krank.
He said he was sick.

5. More cases
Future reference: „werde“ + infinitive. Questions: „ob“ or a question word, with the verb in Konjunktiv I. In spoken language the indicative is often used.

Er sagte, er werde morgen kommen.
He said he would come tomorrow.

Sie fragte, ob er Zeit habe.
She asked whether he had time.

Er sagt, er ist krank. (umgangssprachlich)
He says he is ill. (colloquial)

explanation.en:
Verbs become nouns — this makes the style more objective and compact.
With endings such as -ung or -nis (prüfen → die Prüfung), without an ending (schließen → der Abschluss) or as an infinitive with „das“ (das Prüfen). Typical of reports and formal texts.
Example: Nach Abschluss der Prüfung … (statt: Nachdem die Prüfung abgeschlossen wurde …)
After completion of the exam … (instead of: After the exam was completed …)

rule.en:
1. Three ways to form nouns from verbs
WayFormation
Ending -ungverb stem + -ung (feminine)
prüfen → die Prüfung
to check → the examination
beachten → die Beachtung
to observe → the observance
Ending -nisverb stem + -nis (mostly neuter)
ergeben → das Ergebnis
to yield → the result
erleben → das Erlebnis
to experience → the experience
Stem noun without an ending (often with a vowel change)verb stem, gender varies
schließen → der Abschluss
to close → the completion
steigen → der Anstieg
to rise → the increase
beginnen → der Beginn
to begin → the beginning
Nominalised infinitivedas + infinitive (neuter)
prüfen → das Prüfen
to check → the checking
lesen → das Lesen
to read → reading


The endings „-heit“ and „-keit“ form nouns from adjectives (schön → die Schönheit), not from verbs.

2. Learning the gender
-ung is always feminine. -nis is mostly neuter (das Ergebnis) but not always (die Erlaubnis). The nominalised infinitive is neuter. With stem nouns the gender varies — it is best to learn the noun together with its article.

3. Typical transformation: subordinate clause → noun phrase
A whole subordinate clause with a conjunction can often be shortened to a preposition + nominalisation — typical of formal style.

Subordinate clauseNominal style
Nachdem die Prüfung abgeschlossen wurde, …
After the exam was completed, …		Nach Abschluss der Prüfung, …
After completion of the exam, …
Weil die Kosten gestiegen sind, …
Because the costs have risen, …		Wegen des Anstiegs der Kosten, …
Because of the rise in costs, …
Wenn man die Regeln beachtet, …
If the rules are observed, …		Bei Beachtung der Regeln, …
When observing the rules, …
Bevor der Vertrag unterzeichnet wird, …
Before the contract is signed, …		Vor Unterzeichnung des Vertrags, …
Before signing the contract, …

4. Subject and object → genitive
What was the subject or object in the subordinate clause becomes a genitive attribute after the noun in nominal style:

die Kosten steigen → der Anstieg der Kosten
the costs rise → the rise in costs

man beachtet die Regeln → die Beachtung der Regeln
the rules are observed → the observance of the rules

5. When to use it?
Typical of reports, academic texts, instructions and official language. In everyday speech nominal style often sounds too stiff — subordinate clauses are more natural there.

explanation.en:
Small words that change the tone — not the content.
They occur mainly in spoken language and can rarely be translated literally: „doch“ (emphasis), „ja“ (known / surprised), „mal“ (softer), „eben / halt“ (that is just how it is), „denn“ (interest in questions), „schon“ (reassurance).
Example: Komm doch mal vorbei!
Why not drop by sometime!

rule.en:
Overview of the most important modal particles

ParticleEffect
dochemphasis, reminder, contradiction
Das weißt du doch!
You know that, don't you!
Komm doch mit!
Do come along!
jasomething is known — or: surprise
Du weißt ja, dass ich pünktlich bin.
As you know, I am punctual.
Das ist ja toll!
Well, that's great!
malcasual, softens requests
Komm mal her.
Come here for a moment.
Zeig mal!
Show me!
eben / halt„that is just how it is, nothing can be done“
Das ist eben so.
That's just how it is.
So ist es halt.
That's the way it is.
dennfriendly interest (only in questions)
Wie geht es dir denn?
So how are you?
schonreassurance, confidence
Das wird schon klappen.
It'll work out, don't worry.

1. Position in the sentence
Modal particles stand in the middle field — usually right after the conjugated verb and pronouns, never at the beginning of the sentence:

Kannst du mir mal helfen?
Can you help me for a moment?

2. Combinations are possible
Several particles can occur together and strengthen the tone:

Komm doch mal vorbei! (freundlicher als: „Komm vorbei!“)
Why not drop by sometime! (friendlier than: „Come over!“)

3. Modal particle or identical-sounding word?
Many modal particles also exist as ordinary words. The particle is unstressed and only changes the tone; the ordinary word has a meaning of its own and is stressed. For example, „doch“ as an answer to a negative question is not a particle but an answer word that contradicts:

Kommst du nicht mit? — Doch, ich komme mit.
Aren't you coming? — Yes, I am coming.

Ich habe schon gegessen. (schon = bereits, keine Partikel)
I have already eaten. (schon = already, not a particle)

Das wird schon klappen. (Partikel: Beruhigung)
It'll work out. (particle: reassurance)

4. Style and the workplace
Modal particles are very common in spoken language and casual messages; in formal reports, contracts and letters they are rare. At work they suit friendly requests above all:

Schauen Sie sich das doch bitte mal an.
Please take a look at this when you have a moment.

explanation.en:
Participles can stand before a noun like adjectives.
Participle I (infinitive + -d) describes something simultaneous and active; participle II usually describes a result and is often passive. Both take the normal adjective ending.
Example: das lachende Kind / das gebackene Brot
the laughing child / the baked bread

rule.en:
1. Partizip I — active, simultaneous
Formation: infinitive + „-d“ (lachen → lachend). Describes what is happening right now, usually from the perspective of the person performing the action:
das lachende Kind
the child who is currently laughing
der schlafende Mann
the sleeping man

2. Partizip II — mostly passive, completed
Formed the same way as in the perfect tense (ge-...-t / ge-...-en). Describes the result of an action (usually one the object underwent from outside):
das gebackene Brot
the bread that was baked
der reparierte Wagen
the repaired car

ParticipleMeaning
Partizip Iactive, happening right now
das lachende Kind
the laughing child
Partizip IIpassive / completed, result
das gebackene Brot
the baked bread

3. Declined like a normal adjective
Before a noun, the participle takes the usual adjective ending, depending on the article, case, and gender: der lachende Mann, die lachende Frau, dem lachenden Kind.

4. Extended participial construction
A participle can be expanded with further information and then stands entirely before the noun — typical of formal / written texts:
der vor Kurzem eingestellte Mitarbeiter
the employee hired recently
(instead of: der Mitarbeiter, der vor Kurzem eingestellt wurde)

5. Special cases
zu + participle I means „must / can be …-ed“. Participle II of verbs without an accusative object (steigen, ankommen) is active:

die zu lösende Aufgabe (= die Aufgabe, die gelöst werden muss)
the task to be solved

der gestiegene Preis (= der Preis, der gestiegen ist)
the price that has risen

explanation.en:
„Während“ is either a connector or a preposition.
With its own verb (subordinate clause, verb at the end) it is a connector; before a noun in the genitive it is a preposition. Wegen, trotz, aufgrund, innerhalb and außerhalb + genitive work the same way.
Example: Während er arbeitet, hört er Musik. / während des Meetings
While he works, he listens to music. / during the meeting

rule.en:
1. „Während“ as a connector (subordinate clause)
Introduces a whole subordinate clause with its own verb — verb at the end of the clause:
Während er arbeitet, hört er Musik.
While he works, he listens to music.

2. „Während“ as a preposition + genitive
Stands directly before a noun in the genitive, with no verb of its own:
während des Meetings
during the meeting
während der Woche
during the week

FunctionFeature
Connectorown subordinate clause, verb at the end
Während er arbeitet, hört er Musik.
While he works, he listens to music.
Preposition + genitiveno verb, just a noun in the genitive
während des Meetings
during the meeting

3. Other genitive prepositions with the same structure
PrepositionMeaning
wegenreason
wegen des Regens
because of the rain
trotzconcession / contrast
trotz der Kälte
despite the cold
aufgrundreason (more formal)
aufgrund der Lage
on the basis of the situation
innerhalb / außerhalbtime / space-limited
innerhalb einer Woche
within a week

4. Colloquial usage: genitive prepositions + dative
In spoken German you'll often hear „wegen dem Regen“ (dative) instead of „wegen des Regens“ (genitive) — but in formal / written German and on exams, the genitive is always the standard.

5. „Während“ can also express a contrast
As a connector „während“ can express not only simultaneity but also a contrast („wohingegen“):

Er ist fleißig, während sein Bruder faul ist.
He is hard-working, whereas his brother is lazy.

6. Genitive ending and „von“
Masculine and neuter nouns take -(e)s in the genitive: des Regens, des Meetings. A plural without an article often takes „von“ + dative:

wegen des Regens
because of the rain

innerhalb von zwei Wochen
within two weeks
